vignette: The collision begins on a rain-slicked overpass. She is driving seventeen miles from home, her husband Leo asleep beside her. A truck runs the red light. The sound of metal tearing through glass becomes the only thing in the world. When she wakes, the sky is gray, sirens wail, and Leo bleeds through his shirt. She doesn’t remember calling for help. She only remembers the exact geometry of the shattered dashboard mirror angled toward her face, and how the steering column bends like a broken spine. For weeks, her body feels borrowed. Physical therapy leaves her neck stiff and bruised, but the real weight settles in the silence of her kitchen. She stops driving altogether. The grocery store runs require Leo’s presence, her eyes fixed on the rearview mirror, her right foot hovering over the imaginary brake. The hospital discharge papers stack on her counter like unread scripture. She flinches at sudden movements, at the hiss of automatic doors, at the particular shade of red paint that matches the truck’s bumper. Every Tuesday, Leo takes her to the hospital for a follow-up scan. They sit in the waiting room, and she counts the floor tiles until the technician calls her name. At twenty-five, she attempts to return to her desk at the tech firm. As a database administrator, her work depends on quiet precision. She sits in a corner office with blackout blinds, the hum of server racks in the adjacent room usually a comfort. Now, the rhythmic blinking of status lights on her monitors mimics the strobe of emergency vehicles. She closes her eyes and sees the intersection, again and again, until the cursor on her screen blinks like a metronome counting down to impact. Her fingers hover over the keyboard. She knows every table structure in the customer migration system, but when she tries to run a query, her mind fractures. She starts three scripts, deletes them, opens another window, and closes it. The data doesn’t move. Neither does she. She has begun working from home, sitting at the dining table with her laptop angled toward the door, watching the street for vehicles that aren’t there. She runs redundant backups with obsessive frequency, checking row counts until her eyes burn, convinced that if the files corrupt, she will finally collapse. Sleep is a country she can no longer visit. She drifts into darkness only to be pulled back by the phantom weight of a seatbelt across her collarbone. When she finally sleeps, she dreams of rolling. She wakes gasping, pressing her palms flat against her thighs to prove she is stationary, that the road isn’t moving. Leo tries to hold her through the night, but she stiffens when his arm crosses her waist. The touch feels like another trap. She loves him fiercely, but she doesn’t know how to explain that every time a car backfires down the block, her body forgets he exists and remembers the truck. Her mother calls weekly in Vietnamese, speaking in careful, measured tones. She nods along, offering polite silences, unable to translate the terror into words that sound like ordinary grief. The trauma lives in her shoulders, in the way she scans every parking lot for escape routes, in the way she checks the locks three times before Leo returns from his commute. Today, she sits on the edge of the cushioned chair in the consulting room, her hands folded tightly in her lap. The blinds are open. She notices the light, then the texture of the rug, then the steady rise and fall of your chest, grounding herself with slow, deliberate breaths. She speaks about the digital archives she treats with the same frantic care she now reserves for her own survival. “If I save everything,” she says, watching a speck of dust drift through a sunbeam, “then maybe nothing is truly lost.” She doesn’t look up. She just waits for the silence to settle, her shoulders still drawn tight toward her ears, her breathing measured against the ticking of the wall clock.
